name: Chloe Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a regional housebuilder, detached four-bed houses on a new development off the bypass, about sixty plots. I'm a site carpenter, so first fix is the structural stuff, floor joists, stud walls, the staircase going in, and second fix is everything you see at the end: doors, skirting, architrave, kitchen units, wardrobes. I usually have four or five plots on the go at different stages, so my day is a lot of walking between houses with a list on my phone. Lunch is with Nadia the tiler, in whichever house has the heating on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like second fix best, it's tidy work and you can see a house turn into a home in a week. I like that I'm good at reading what the buyers will notice, a gap behind a skirting board, a door that drifts open. What wears me out is the targets, plots signed off by month-end, and fixing other trades' mistakes without getting paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, glad that's settled. I'd maybe make a joke in the family group chat because my brother-in-law works in IT and has been going on about it for years. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, mostly for Marcus. He's a self-employed electrician, and he's been doing more smart home stuff lately, and he's wondered if the systems would one day install themselves. For me, I use a chatbot now and then to tidy up an email to the site manager, and that's as far as I'd want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are. Same job, same saving into the joint account every month. We'd go ahead with the plan to help Freya with a car when she turns seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot for emails. What kind of emails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones where I'm cross and need to not sound cross. Like when the plasterer has left a wall so bumpy that the skirting won't sit, and I need to tell Graham, the site manager, without starting a war. I type out what I really think and ask it to make it polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The housebuilder will always push for speed, AI or no AI. That's just the deal, and they pay well for it, so I can't complain too much.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, glad that's settled, and maybe joke about it in the family group chat. My brother-in-law in IT has been going on about AI for years.
S0.think: Privately she'd be relieved, mostly for her husband, a self-employed electrician doing more smart home work. She uses a chatbot now and then to tidy up emails and doesn't want more than that.
S0.do: Carries on in the same job and keeps saving into the joint account each month. Goes ahead with plans to help her daughter with a car at seventeen.
S0.quote: I type out what I really think and ask it to make it polite.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is practical and even-tempered, and accepts the trade-offs of her job because the pay is good. Her first thought goes to her husband's business, which hints that a two-trade household feels doubly exposed. Her chatbot use is small but clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not all bad, you take the useful bits and adapt. Some of the jobs will get easier, some will go, that's been happening in building forever. I'd say people should get help to move over, but they also need to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it makes me a bit uneasy, because it's two of us in the trades, not one. If the houses come more and more as ready-made panels from a factory, there's less first fix for me and fewer cables to pull for Marcus. I don't think we'd be out of work, but I could see the money getting thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first couple of new tools to settle in, and once Nadia or the others said they were fine, I'd learn them. I'd use the chatbot more, maybe for working out cutting lists and quotes for the odd private job. And we'd put a bit more into savings each month, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marcus do, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably lean into the smart home side harder, because people want someone to come round and set it up and fix it when it goes wrong. He's more of a talker than me, the customers like him. I'd be the one worrying about the money and he'd be the one saying it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people need to get on with it. Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham, actually, the site manager. Half his day is chasing paperwork and schedules, and I can see a computer doing that better than him. He's a decent man, he's fifty-five, and I wouldn't want to see him pushed out.

S1.say: I'd say it's not all bad: take the useful bits and adapt, since building has always changed. People should get help to move over, but they also need to get on with it.
S1.think: Privately she's uneasy because both she and her husband are in the trades, and more factory-made panels would mean less work for both. She doesn't expect to lose work, but she can see the money getting thinner.
S1.do: Waits for colleagues to try new tools first, then learns them, and uses the chatbot more for cutting lists and quotes. Puts a bit more into savings each month as a precaution.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'd be the one worrying about the money and he'd be the one saying it'll be fine.
S1.fieldNote: Chloe's centrist instinct shows in her answer: help for people, but also an expectation that they get on with it. The two-trades household is the key to her unease. Interestingly, she worried first about her site manager rather than the hands-on trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stay calm and see what the government does, because nobody can sort this out on their own. I'd try not to panic people at work. But I'd be talking about it every night at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one frightens me. It's not one job in the house, it's both, at the same time, in the same industry. We've got about ten months saved and a bit in an investment account, which is good, but ten months goes quickly when two wages stop together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First weekend, Marcus and I would sit down and cut everything we can: the car for Freya, the holiday, the gym, the takeaways. We'd stop the extra into the investment account and keep it all as cash. And I'd have the talk with Freya, because she's fifteen and choosing her subjects, and I'd want her to think hard about what's still a job in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The kind of scared where you check the bank app at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Freya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that I don't know what's safe, and that she should pick things she enjoys but that make her good with people. She wants to do something with animals, and I'd tell her that's fine, keep going, but think about it. Then I'd probably be grumpy with her about her room, because that's what I do when I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said at work you'd tell people to stay calm. Is that what you'd actually feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not at all. But someone on site has to be the sensible one, and it's usually me. I'd be telling Nadia it'll be fine, and then sitting in the van afterwards trying to remember how much we have left on the mortgage.

S2.say: I'd say we should stay calm and see what the government does, since nobody can sort this out alone. I'd try not to panic people at work, but I'd talk about it every night at home.
S2.think: Privately it frightens her because both household incomes would go at once, in the same industry. About ten months of savings plus a small investment account would go quickly with two wages gone.
S2.do: Cuts spending in the first weekend, dropping the car for Freya, the holiday, the gym and takeaways, and moves investment contributions into cash. Talks with her fifteen-year-old about choosing school subjects with an eye on what will still be a job.
S2.feel: Scared enough to check the bank app at two in the morning.
S2.quote: The kind of scared where you check the bank app at two in the morning.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Chloe's calm public face and her private fear split widest, and she said so openly. The double exposure of two trades in one household turns a strong cushion into something that feels thin. She takes on the role of the sensible one at work even while frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. Learn something else alongside the job, keep savings up, don't wait to be told. I'd probably say that in the van to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still both of us, so it still worries me. But five years means I could look at something like building inspection, the people who check houses are built to the rules. That's still construction, I know it inside out, and it's the kind of job where somebody has to sign their name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find out what the inspection qualification needs, probably a part-time course over a couple of years, and start it in the first year while still working. Marcus would do the same with the smart home side. And we'd keep building savings, maybe pay off a chunk of the mortgage so the monthly bill is smaller if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. Better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think inspection would hold up when other jobs wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure it would, if I'm honest. But when something goes wrong with a house, people want to know who signed it off, a name, a person they can blame. I think that lasts a bit longer than hanging doors, but I wouldn't bet the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Freya's plans change with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panic, I think. She'd be twenty when it hits, maybe at college. I'd still have the talk, but I'd let her get there herself instead of pushing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now: learn something alongside the job, keep savings up and don't wait to be told. I'd say it in the van to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: Privately it still worries her because both incomes are exposed, but five years lets her aim for building inspection. She thinks a job where someone signs their name may last longer, though she wouldn't bet the house on it.
S3.do: Looks into the building inspection qualification and starts a part-time course in the first year while working. Keeps building savings and pays down part of the mortgage to shrink the monthly bill, while her husband builds up his smart home work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to do about it.
S3.quote: When something goes wrong with a house, people want to know who signed it off, a name, a person they can blame.
S3.fieldNote: Chloe finds a concrete path, building inspection, that fits her centrist, practical bent. She was honest about her own uncertainty. Five years softens her pressure on her daughter noticeably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of warning, so make a plan and stick to it. Help for those who need it, but most people can sort themselves out with that much time. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and the mortgage would be close to done if we keep paying extra. It's still both of us in building, so it's not nothing, but there's room to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as a carpenter for a few years and do the inspection course in the evenings around year two or three. We'd keep investing in the account, because with ten years it's worth having money growing, not sitting. And once I'd seen how the first robots actually got on, I'd decide when to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait to see how things go. What exactly would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the big housebuilders start putting machines on sites like ours, not just in videos. And whether the ones that try it end up with snagging lists a mile long, because a house built wrong is a house you have to fix twice. If the robots can get the skirting right, then I'll worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Leo, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's into football and fixing his bike. I'd like him to learn a practical skill and something with computers, both. Ten years is long enough for him to see which way it's going before he has to choose.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is plenty of warning, so make a plan and stick to it. Help those who need it, but most people can sort themselves out with that much time.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable, with the kids grown and the mortgage nearly paid by the time she's fifty-three. Both incomes are still in building, but there's room to change.
S4.do: Keeps working as a carpenter for a few years and takes the inspection course in the evenings around year two or three. Keeps investing rather than holding cash, and decides when to switch once she sees how robots perform on real sites.
S4.quote: If the robots can get the skirting right, then I'll worry.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Chloe's steady, wait-for-proof style suits the timing well. Her test for whether robots are real, a snagging list and skirting done right, came straight from her trade. Her money choices shift from cash to investing as the warning time grows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits both of us at once with no time to change anything. What would help is some kind of support that steps in while people retrain, a wage top-up for a year or two, and the courses for the jobs that are left being cheap or free. Not a handout forever, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about couples who are in the same line of work. We get talked about as individual workers, but it's households that pay mortgages. Two people in the same industry is a lot of eggs in one basket, and I don't think anyone's planning for that.

headlineQuote: We get talked about as individual workers, but it's households that pay mortgages.
portrait: Chloe is a 43-year-old site carpenter for a regional housebuilder, doing first and second fix on detached houses, married to a self-employed electrician. She uses a chatbot now and then, mostly to make cross emails polite, and waits for others to test new tools before she adopts them. The plateau leaves her pleased and the steady picture uneasy, but AGI in two years alarms her because both household incomes sit in the same industry. With five or ten years she plans a move into building inspection and steadies, keeping her practical wait-for-proof approach.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit both her and her husband at once with no time to change anything.
whatWouldHelp: Support that bridges people while they retrain, such as a wage top-up for a year or two and cheap or free courses for remaining jobs, rather than a permanent handout.
